THE ROLE

You join the Platform team, which designs and builds the ZKsync OS node. You own one or more of its core systems end to end: peer-to-peer networking, consensus, RPC, the sequencer or storage, depending on where your depth is. We are looking first for depth in consensus or peer-to-peer networking, and next in high-performance storage. You also bring new protocol features into the node, such as cross-chain interoperability and new zero-knowledge provers.

 - Integrate new protocol features. Bring features such as interoperability and new provers into the node without breaking existing behaviour or the upgrade path.

 - Design bugs out. Use the type system, architecture, property-based testing and fuzzing so whole classes of bugs never reach production.

 - Hold the review bar. Review your colleagues' code as carefully as you write your own, and expect the same from them.

 - Use AI with judgment. Use the best AI tools to move faster, and understand every line you merge, whoever or whatever wrote it.

 - Your code reviews find real problems, and you can explain every line you ship.

 - You can take a protocol change from specification to a running system without breaking what already works.

Nice to have: Ethereum execution or consensus client internals; RocksDB or another high-performance storage engine; zero-knowledge provers; libp2p or a comparable networking stack; open-source systems work we can read.

* Reliability & maintainability: Build the platform so it stays robust and serviceable across the product's life, under the conditions a defense product actually faces.

About the project: CLARA (Cognitive Layered Agentic Reasoning for ARIS) is a three-year, Genesis Mission Phase II project led by Northeastern University with MSU/FRIB and Gravitate AI. It will build an agentic AI system for operating the Advanced Rare Isotope Separator (ARIS) at FRIB. ARIS operations are limited by the gap between LISE++ simulations and observed beam behavior. As a result, weekly beam development takes 16 to 24 hours, about half of which goes to manual isotope calibration. Planning a new experiment takes about 20 days, and no predictive monitoring exists for roughly 200 time-correlated machine parameters.
  
  
**CLARA Addresses This With Three Objectives**

* Planning and tuning. Bayesian optimization uses LISE++ as a physics-informed prior, alongside paired forward and inverse neural surrogates trained on simulation and EPICS archive data. These power a Planning Agent for non-experts and an Expert Tuning Agent.
* Calibration. Diffeomorphic image registration maps simulated particle identification (PID) distributions to measured ones from a single measurement.
* Monitoring and knowledge. Quickest Change Detection models (classical CuSum and a transformer-based DeepQCD) and a hazardous-configuration classifier make up a Safety Agent with gated beam-interrupt authority. A Critic module commits validated tunes to a knowledge graph built with eGoT.

The targets are reducing experiment planning time to 1 to 2 days, beam development time to about 4 hours, and thus facilitating 500 to 800 extra beam hours per year. The project aims to advance from TRL 3 to TRL 6–7 and to validate transfer to at least one non-ARIS separator.
